analysis.one_liner: Mandates more oil, gas, and coal leasing on federal lands, speeds pipeline and export permits, and locks in loosened environmental rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referrals and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the Interior Department to hold at least four oil and gas lease sales a year in ten states and to sell all eligible parcels, restart and expand offshore lease sales in the Gulf of Mexico and Alaska, and make drilling permits近乎 automatic if not decided within 30 to 60 days. It would fast-track natural gas pipelines and exports, and it would reinstate several 2020-era rules that narrowed water and methane protections — then bar federal agencies from changing them for 15 years. It also opens offshore mining of hardrock minerals, possibly at a zero royalty rate.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies get guaranteed lease sales across ten states, drilling permits deemed approved if the government misses a 60-day deadline, and natural gas export applications from 2020 through 2025 deemed approved automatically. Pipeline and LNG developers get one-year approval deadlines and certificates issued without further proceedings if safety rules are met. Coal and hardrock mining companies get bans on executive-branch moratoria and new offshore mining licenses with a royalty rate the Secretary could set at zero. Geothermal, solar, and wind developers get designated priority leasing areas and a categorical exclusion from environmental review for geothermal exploration.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil, gas, coal, and mining companies

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Interior Department to hold at least 4 oil and gas lease sales annually in each of ten states, offering all eligible parcels, with replacement sales if any sale is canceled [S2] [S3].

Bars the President from imposing any moratorium on new oil, gas, coal, or critical mineral leasing on federal land — including the outer continental shelf — unless Congress passes a law authorizing it [S3].
Deems all natural gas export applications submitted between January 1, 2020 and January 1, 2025 approved, and requires export decisions within 60 days [S3].

Requires the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to act on pipeline applications within one year, and lets it issue pipeline certificates without further proceedings if the project meets safety regulations [S3].
Makes drilling permit applications automatically approved if the Interior Department does not decide within 60 days, and sets a 30-day decision deadline with only limited extensions [S3].
Designates federal priority areas for geothermal, solar, and wind leasing and requires lease sales for those areas within a year of designation [S2] [S3].
Supporters argued that predictable leasing and permitting would increase domestic energy production and competition, lowering energy prices [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would bear the cost of selling every eligible parcel on federal land, and could receive as little as zero royalties on new offshore hardrock mining if the Secretary finds that necessary for competition. Communities near drilling, pipelines, and mining would live with a narrowed National Environmental Policy Act that only examines impacts inside the United States, no presidential permit requirement for cross-border pipelines, and 2020-era rules weakening Clean Water Act and methane protections frozen in place for 15 years. Federal agencies would lose the ability to update those rules in response to new science or court rulings.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and communities near energy development

drawbacks.text: The bill reinstates the 2020 Navigable Waters Protection Rule, a 2020 methane rule, and the 2020 NEPA rule, and prohibits any agency from modifying them for 15 years — locking in regulations through statutory handcuffs rather than the normal rulemaking process [S3].
It amends the National Environmental Policy Act so federal reviews examine only effects 'in the United States', narrowing the scope of environmental analysis for projects with spillover effects [S3].
It allows offshore hardrock mineral licenses with a royalty rate the Secretary could set at 0 percent, and grants noncompetitive exploration and mining licenses on the outer continental shelf [S3].
Requiring a minimum of two offshore lease sales per year in Alaska, on top of mandated onshore sales in ten states, would open areas that current administrations have withheld from leasing [S2] [S3].
The bill strips the executive branch — including future presidents of either party — of authority to pause leasing or withdraw land from energy development without a new act of Congress [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters made a real argument in 2022: with gasoline and natural gas prices high after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, more leasing and faster permitting could add supply and lower prices. But the bill's core provisions mostly hand operational control to industry — mandatory lease sales of every eligible parcel, permits deemed approved on a deadline, exports deemed approved retroactively, and 15-year freezes on environmental and methane rules — while cutting federal royalty receipts and limiting environmental review. The energy-price benefit is indirect and unguaranteed; the deregulation and revenue concessions are direct.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four House committees and three subcommittees in March 2022, none of them ever took it up, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. August Pfluger (R-TX) introduced the Energy Freedom Act on March 15, 2022, with 8 Republican cosponsors [S1] [S4].

The Speaker referred it to four committees at once — Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Agriculture — meaning no single committee had clear custody and each had to act on the parts in its jurisdiction [S5].
Within two days it was sent to three subcommittees (Energy; Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials; Water Resources and Environment), the last recorded action in its history [S5].
No committee markup, report, floor vote, or Senate action ever followed; the bill died on January 3, 2023, when the 117th Congress ended [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the 2020 water, methane, and NEPA rules were not reinstated and frozen for 15 years, no offshore mining licenses with possible zero royalties were created, and no president of either party lost the authority to pause federal energy leasing. Communities near public lands and the agencies' environmental review authority are better off; the oil, gas, coal, pipeline, and mining companies that would have gained the bill's leasing mandates and permitting deadlines gained nothing from it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public lands and environmental review; industry gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support; with Democrats controlling the House, the bill never advanced past referral, though it never reached a vote that would have shown the full partisan split.

industries.note: The bill mandates at least four lease sales a year in ten states offering all eligible parcels, deems drilling permits approved after 60 days, and deems all 2020-2025 export applications approved. The public benefit supporters cite — lower energy prices — is indirect, while the industry gains guaranteed access to public resources on set terms.

industries.industry: Natural gas pipeline and LNG export developers
industries.note: One-year approval deadlines for pipeline authorizations, certificates issued without further proceedings if safety rules are met, no presidential permit for cross-border pipelines, and retroactively approved export applications shorten the review process that lets affected communities and agencies weigh in.
The bill bans any presidential moratorium on new coal leasing on federal land without an act of Congress, insulating coal leasing from future administrations.
New noncompetitive exploration and mining licenses on the outer continental shelf, with a royalty rate the Secretary could set at zero percent, would transfer minerals with minimal public return.

The bill designates federal priority leasing areas for renewable projects and categorically excludes geothermal exploration tests from environmental review — a genuine boost to clean energy buildout, though the same shortcut bypasses site-specific review.
